steps.observation: You have 900 seconds. How does a transformer neural network work, conceptually?

steps.action:
Here’s a high-level, step-by-step picture of how a Transformer works conceptually:

1. Input Representation  
   • You start with a sequence of tokens (words, subwords, etc.).  
   • Each token is mapped to a continuous vector via an embedding table.  
   • Because the model is “position-agnostic,” you add a positional encoding (fixed or learned) so it knows each token’s order.

2. Self-Attention Mechanism  
   At the heart of the Transformer is self-attention, which lets each position in the sequence look at (attend to) other positions. For each token position:  
   • You linearly project its embedding into three vectors: Query (Q), Key (K), and Value (V).  
   • You compute attention weights by taking the dot-product of Q with every K in the sequence, scaling by √d, and applying softmax.  
   • You multiply those weights by the corresponding Vs and sum them to get a new representation for that position.  
   This lets each token gather information from anywhere in the sequence, weighted by relevance.

3. Multi-Head Attention  
   Instead of one attention operation, you run several in parallel (“heads”), each with different projection matrices.  
   • Each head captures different aspects of relationships (syntax, semantics, distances, etc.).  
   • You concatenate all heads’ outputs and project back to the model dimension.

4. Feed-Forward Network and Residuals  
   After multi-head attention comes a position-wise feed-forward network (the same two-layer MLP applied independently at each position).  
   • Typically: Linear → ReLU (or GELU) → Linear.  
   Around both the multi-head block and the feed-forward block you have:  
   • A residual (skip) connection: you add the block’s input to its output.  
   • Layer normalization to stabilize training.

5. Stacking Layers  
   You stack N identical layers of (multi-head self-attention → feed-forward).  
   In an encoder-decoder Transformer (e.g. for translation), the encoder is a stack of these layers. The decoder has:  
   • Masked self-attention (prevents peeking at future tokens)  
   • Encoder-decoder attention (lets the decoder attend to encoder outputs)  
   • Feed-forward, with its own residuals and norms.

6. Output Projection  
   • In language modeling you typically tie a linear projection from the final layer back to the token-vocabulary space, followed by softmax to get next-token probabilities.  
   • In classification you might pool or take the first token’s vector, then pass it through another MLP to get class logits.

Why It Works So Well  
• Parallelism: Unlike RNNs, all positions are processed simultaneously.  
• Flexibility: Self-attention learns arbitrary token dependencies without regard to distance.  
• Scalability: You can stack many layers and heads, and leverage optimized matrix multiplications.

In under the hood math, every operation is just linear projections, softmaxes, point-wise feed-forwards, additions, and normalizations—yet this architecture is powerful enough to model language, images, and other sequential or structured data.
